references.text: Joseph says that dream interpretation belongs to God, which explains why Egypt's wise men could not interpret Pharaoh's dream.
Joseph points to God as the source of dream interpretation, in contrast to Egypt's wise men who could not provide an answer.
Egypt's magicians (chartummim, the same Hebrew word as in Gen 41:8) are mentioned in connection with Moses and Pharaoh.
Nebuchadnezzar is troubled in spirit after a dream and calls for wise men to interpret it, closely parallel to Pharaoh.
Daniel explains that no wise man can reveal the secret, but God in heaven can—parallel to how no one could interpret for Pharaoh.
Nebuchadnezzar summons all the wise men who cannot interpret the dream, a direct parallel to Pharaoh's experience.
Egypt's wise counselors give foolish advice; Isaiah asks where the wise are who can tell what the Lord has planned—a thematic parallel to the failure of the wise men.
Direct narrative confirmation that no human wisdom could solve the riddle before God intervened.
Direct continuation showing the transition from human distress to divine clarification.
A clear typological parallel between Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar regarding the powerlessness of human wisdom.
A striking parallel in action: the king's call to all wise men to solve an incomprehensible dream.
Nearly word-for-word parallel confirming that 'troubled in spirit' is the common trigger for divine revelation.
Part of the same typological pattern where a king summons all his wise men to solve a riddle.
